title: The Cipher of Little Hawley
premise: Beatrix Nakamura, the observant concierge of Little Hawley's Grand Meridian Hotel, is hired by a nervous stranger who pays triple to prove that a murder scheduled for the town's founding anniversary will not happen. As Beatrix investigates, they discover the 'future murder' mirrors an unsolved death from thirty years ago, and every alibi in Little Hawley was quietly rebuilt around it. The client turns out to be the presumed-dead victim's child, testing whether Beatrix's loyalty to their found family of hotel staff and townsfolk can survive the truth: the killer is Beatrix's own mentor, the hotel's beloved head porter, who has spent three decades protecting a daughter from her father's violence. In the end, Beatrix closes the case by refusing to let history repeat — exposing the old crime, sparing the daughter, and choosing truth over the comfortable lies that made them belong.
about_author: Edmund Okafor is a former night auditor at coastal hotels across three continents, where he collected the small betrayals and quiet kindnesses of hospitality workers. He writes mysteries from a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage, insisting that every locked room is just a lobby nobody watched closely enough.

chapters.title: The Guest Who Paid in Advance
chapters.summary: Beatrix Nakamura, POV. A pale stranger checks into the Grand Meridian, pays for a week upfront, and asks Beatrix to prevent a murder that hasn't happened yet, offering no name or date beyond 'the anniversary.' Beatrix, who never takes a case they can't close, accepts against instinct. The beat is uneasy fascination — the hook of an impossible contract.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Lobby Dust
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix combs guest registers and staff gossip, learning the client arrived days before the founding anniversary, when Little Hawley commemorates the 1994 drowning of local magnate Aldous Vane. The emotional beat is creeping recognition that the town's cheerful memory is curated, not honest.

chapters.title: The Head Porter's Keys
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. We meet Silas Marsh, the hotel's head porter and Beatrix's mentor, who taught them to read guests like weather. Their warm banter hides Beatrix's first test: Silas deflects all questions about 1994 with practiced ease. Beat: affection shadowed by doubt.

chapters.title: A Drowning Nobody Mourned
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. At the town archive, Beatrix finds Aldous Vane's death ruled accidental, but the coroner's file is thin as tissue. A librarian mentions the widow left town overnight and never returned. Beat: the thrill of a thread pulled loose.

chapters.title: The Client Vanishes
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. The paying guest misses checkout; housekeeping finds the room untouched, luggage gone, a note reading only 'You're late.' Beatrix realizes the murder may be closer than the anniversary. Beat: cold alarm, stakes sharpened.

chapters.title: Marta Keeps the Books
chapters.summary: Marta Osei, the hotel's night manager and Beatrix's closest friend, POV. Marta covers for Beatrix's absences while noticing their distraction. Through her eyes we see the hotel as a found family — and see Beatrix lying to it for the first time. Beat: loyalty beginning to strain.

chapters.title: The Vane Daughter
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix tracks the widow's daughter, Iris Vane, now a restorer of old photographs in a neighboring county. Iris claims she knows nothing, but her studio holds a restored portrait of Aldous dated weeks before his death. Beat: guarded grief meeting professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Alibis, Freshly Painted
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Interviewing the anniversary committee, Beatrix notices each witness from 1994 tells an identical story, word for word, as if rehearsed. One lets slip a detail — a second set of footprints on the boathouse dock. Beat: the uncanny smoothness of a lie kept warm for decades.

chapters.title: Silas Warns Me Off
chapters.summary: Silas Marsh POV. Silas privately warns Beatrix that some doors in Little Hawley stay shut for good reasons, revealing he knew Aldous Vane personally. His protectiveness reads as mentorship but lands as threat. Beat: love and menace in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Boathouse at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix searches the derelict Vane boathouse and finds a hidden ledger recording payments to four townsmen, dated after the drowning — hush money. Beat: grim vindication turning to dread about what the money bought.

chapters.title: Four Names, Three Graves
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Of the four paid men, two are dead, one vanished, and one remains: councilman Harold Finch, the anniversary's master of ceremonies. Finch receives Beatrix with flawless charm and flawless denials. Beat: the mask of civic respectability.

chapters.title: What Marta Saw in '94
chapters.summary: Marta Osei POV. Marta, then a teenager, remembers the night Aldous died — the hotel full of mourners who weren't grieving, and young Silas carrying a soaked coat inside. She has never told anyone. Beat: memory as burden, silence as kindness.

chapters.title: The Client Returns
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. The stranger reappears, admitting they are Iris Vane's half-brother, born after the widow fled, and that he hired Beatrix because Iris refuses to reopen the past. He believes someone plans to kill Iris before she can testify. Beat: the case gains a human face and a ticking clock.

chapters.title: Iris Breaks
chapters.summary: Iris Vane POV. Confronted with her brother's fear, Iris confesses she came back not to accuse but to forgive — she has spent years restoring photos of her father and suspects he was murdered by someone who loved the town more than the law. Beat: grief reframed as purpose.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Committee
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix attends the committee's rehearsal and watches Finch stage-manage commemoration like a cover-up, scheduling the memorial toast at the exact hour of the drowning. Beatrix realizes the ceremony itself may be the murder's stage. Beat: theatrical unease.

chapters.title: Silas's Soaked Coat
chapters.summary: Marta Osei POV. Marta finally tells Beatrix about the coat, forcing both to consider that Silas was on the dock that night. Beatrix defends him fiercely; Marta watches her friend choose faith over evidence. Beat: the first open crack between the found family.

chapters.title: Harold Finch's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Pressed with the ledger, Finch admits the payments were real but insists they bought silence about an accident, not a murder — then begs Beatrix, with genuine terror, to drop the case before the anniversary. Beat: fear leaking through power.

chapters.title: The Photograph Under the Photograph
chapters.summary: Iris Vane POV. Iris discovers a hidden image beneath a restored photo: Aldous alive on the dock with a woman who is not his wife. The revelation recasts everything — there was another person on the dock that night. Beat: vertigo of revised history.

chapters.title: Eleanor, the Chambermaid Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix identifies the woman: Eleanor Pryce, once a chambermaid, now the proprietor of the tea room, and the only 1994 witness with no alibi on file. Eleanor serves Beatrix tea and tells them, gently, to stop digging. Beat: sweetness wrapped around warning.

chapters.title: Half a Truth from Eleanor
chapters.summary: Eleanor Pryce POV. Eleanor recalls loving Aldous and leaving the dock minutes before he drowned — and recalls who else was watching from the shadows. She names no one, but her account confirms the death was witnessed. Beat: guilt preserved like jam, forty years sealed.

chapters.title: The Case Against My Mentor
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Assembling evidence, Beatrix confronts the possibility that Silas, then a young porter devoted to the Vane household, had means, presence, and motive unexplored. Beatrix tests him with a false detail and catches him correcting it. Beat: heartbreak disguised as deduction.

chapters.title: Marta's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Marta Osei POV. Marta demands Beatrix either trust the family enough to share the case or work alone. Beatrix shares everything except the suspicion of Silas. Marta sees the omission instantly. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made explicit between friends.

chapters.title: The Second Ledger
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. In the hotel's sub-basement archive, Beatrix finds a second ledger in Silas's handwriting — records of anonymous payments made out of his own wages for thirty years, addressed to the Vane widow. Payments, not hush money. Reparations? Beat: whiplash of reinterpretation.

chapters.title: What Silas Was Paying For
chapters.summary: Silas Marsh POV. Silas's chapter reveals partial truth: he saw Aldous die, killed not by a hand but by a struggle he failed to stop, and has paid the widow ever since out of shame for his silence. He still conceals the identity of the other figure on the dock. Beat: guilt with a lockbox around its center.

chapters.title: Threats at the Front Desk
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Anonymous notes begin arriving at the concierge desk, each quoting Beatrix's own investigation back at them, the last reading 'The anniversary is for remembering, not reopening.' Someone inside the hotel is reporting on Beatrix. Beat: paranoia blooming at home.

chapters.title: The Mole in Housekeeping
chapters.summary: Marta Osei POV. Marta sets a trap with planted information and identifies the informant: timid porter Danny, coerced by Finch over an old debt. Danny's tears reveal Finch isn't the top of the chain — he's afraid of someone too. Beat: pity for a small traitor.

chapters.title: Finch Runs
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix confronts Finch with Danny's testimony; within hours Finch attempts to flee town and is stopped — not by police, but by a car blocking the coast road, driven by someone he salutes. Beat: the true power revealed by obedience.

chapters.title: The Founder's Heir
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Following Finch's car, Beatrix learns the figure above him is Cordelia Vane-Ashford, Aldous's sister, matriarch of the anniversary foundation, who has curated the town's memory since 1994. Her alibi that night: hosting the wake. Beat: respectability as fortress.

chapters.title: Cordelia's Version
chapters.summary: Cordelia Vane-Ashford POV. Cordelia admits she arranged the cover-up — not to protect a killer, she claims, but to protect the town and her brother's children from the scandal of what Aldous truly was: violent, bankrupt, and feared. She offers Beatrix a place in that peace. Beat: temptation of the beautiful lie.

chapters.title: The Client's Secret
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix discovers the client's final deception: he is not Iris's brother but Aldous's son by Eleanor Pryce, raised elsewhere, seeking the truth of the father who abandoned him — and possibly the inheritance Cordelia controls. Motive blurs everywhere. Beat: the case folding inward.

chapters.title: Night of the Anniversary
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs — Marta, Silas, Iris. The founding celebration fills the hotel; Cordelia prepares her toast; Iris arrives uninvited with the restored photograph; Silas polishes brass with shaking hands. Beat: converging dread, everyone dressed for a funeral disguised as a festival.

chapters.title: The Toast at the Exact Hour
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. At the stroke of the drowning hour, Cordelia begins her toast — and Beatrix spots the trap: Iris has been maneuvered onto the dark boathouse balcony, alone, exactly where her father died. The predicted murder has a time and place after all. Beat: ice-water clarity.

chapters.title: Race Across the Lawns
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix runs, hampered by celebratory crowds, and reaches the balcony as a hooded figure closes on Iris. Beatrix intervenes; in the scuffle the hood falls — revealing not a killer but Danny, holding a letter, forced again to frighten rather than harm. Beat: relief curdling into confusion.

chapters.title: The Letter That Wasn't a Threat
chapters.summary: Iris Vane POV. The letter Danny carried is from Cordelia to Iris: an offer of the estate in exchange for leaving before the toast. But tucked inside is something Cordelia doesn't know was included — the original coroner's photograph showing Aldous's injuries were defensive. Beat: proof surfacing through malice's own machinery.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Wake Room
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix gathers Cordelia, Finch, Eleanor, Iris, and the client in the same parlor used for the 1994 wake and lays out the reconstruction: Aldous attacked Eleanor on the dock; Cordelia, arriving to confront her brother, struck him to stop him — accidentally killing him — then built thirty years of alibis. Beat: the climax of revelation, every face stripped.

chapters.title: Silas Testifies
chapters.summary: Silas Marsh POV. Silas confirms he witnessed it all and stayed silent to protect Eleanor and the town, his payments penance. He surrenders himself alongside Cordelia, telling Beatrix he taught them to notice everything so that one day they'd notice this. Beat: the mentor's fall and gift entwined.

chapters.title: Arrests at Dawn
chapters.summary: Marta Osei POV. Police take Cordelia and Silas at first light while the town sleeps off its celebration. Marta comforts Beatrix, who cannot decide if closing the case feels like victory or betrayal. Beat: hollow triumph, tenderness offered anyway.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix visits Silas in custody; he refuses regret, only asks that Beatrix keep the hotel's standards high. Beatrix realizes the found family survives not because it hid the truth but because it can hold both truth and love at once. Beat: grief integrated into belonging.

chapters.title: The Cipher Solved
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV. Beatrix decodes the client's original riddle — the 'murder yet to happen' was always the anniversary itself, the yearly reenactment of the lie; proving it wouldn't happen meant ending the ritual of silence. The case closes as designed. Beat: intellectual satisfaction fused with moral weight.

chapters.title: Checkout Time
chapters.summary: Beatrix POV, epilogue tone. Spring comes; Iris restores the hotel's founder portraits honestly, Eleanor keeps pouring tea, Danny stays on probation and gratitude. A new nervous guest approaches the desk with an impossible request, and Beatrix — changed, steadier — says yes. Beat: renewal; the door opens on the next case.
